decks.title: Measures of Central Tendency — Part 1: The Arithmetic Mean
goals: Explain what an average and central tendency mean
Calculate the arithmetic mean of individual, discrete and continuous series by the direct, assumed-mean and step-deviation methods
State the properties, merits and demerits of the arithmetic mean

slides.heading: The Arithmetic Mean
slides.body_md: Part 1 — one **value** that stands for a whole **series**.

nodes.label: Mean of individual and discrete series

visual.alt: Route map of Part 1: what an average is, the mean of individual and discrete series, the mean of a continuous series, the weighted mean, and the properties, merits and demerits of the mean
visual.caption: Part 1 at a glance

slides.narration: A long list of figures is hard to hold in the mind. An average is a single value that stands for the whole set. In this part we learn the most common average, the arithmetic mean. We calculate it for individual, discrete and continuous series, by three methods, and then look at weighted means and the properties of the mean.

slides.heading: What is an average?
slides.body_md: An **average** is a single value that represents a whole set of data. Values tend to gather around a centre, so averages are called measures of **central tendency**.

rows: Sum of the values over their number
Middle value of the arranged series
Arrange, then locate the middle item
Find the value with the highest frequency

visual.alt: Table of the three common averages, the arithmetic mean, the median and the mode, with what each is and how it is found

slides.narration: An average is one value that represents the whole data. In most data the values gather around a centre, so averages are called measures of central tendency. We study three of them. The arithmetic mean divides the total by the number of items. The median is the middle value. The mode is the value that occurs most often.

slides.heading: Mean of an individual series
slides.body_md: The **arithmetic mean** is the sum of all observations divided by their number. Direct method: X̄ = ΣX ÷ N. Assumed-mean method: X̄ = A + Σd ÷ N, where d = X − A.

visual.alt: Table of the daily rainfall of the imagined Dhunmarg hill station over ten days, 12, 8, 15, 9, 20, 6, 10, 14, 11, 5 millimetres with total 110, and the deviations from an assumed mean of 10, 2, -2, 5, -1, 10, -4, 0, 4, 1, -5 with total 10
visual.caption: Imagined Dhunmarg hill station, millimetres.

slides.narration: Here are daily rainfall figures of an imagined hill station, Dhunmarg, over ten days. For the direct method, add all the values and divide by the number of days. For the assumed mean method, pick a convenient value, find how far each observation lies from it, add those deviations, and correct the assumed value by the average deviation.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: rainfall at Dhunmarg
slides.body_md: Find the mean daily rainfall of the imagined Dhunmarg hill station by both methods.
bullets: Step 3 — Assumed mean A = 10: the deviations are 2, -2, 5, -1, 10, -4, 0, 4, 1, -5, so Σd = 10.

visual.alt: Table of the mean rainfall of the imagined Dhunmarg hill station by the direct method and by the assumed-mean method, both 11 millimetres
visual.caption: Both methods give the same mean.

slides.narration: Adding the ten rainfall figures gives 110. Dividing by ten days gives a mean of 11 millimetres. Now take ten as the assumed mean. The deviations add up to 10, and ten plus 10 over ten gives the same mean, 11. Both methods must agree.

slides.heading: Quick check: mean of rainfall
slides.body_md: Find the mean daily rainfall of another imagined hill station.
slides.narration: Add up all the daily rainfall figures given in the question. Then divide the total by the number of days. Give your answer in millimetres, correct to two decimal places if needed.

slides.heading: Formulae at a glance
slides.body_md: In a **discrete series** each value X occurs f times, so X̄ = ΣfX ÷ Σf.

visual.alt: Table of the formulae for the arithmetic mean of individual, discrete and continuous series by the direct, assumed-mean and step-deviation methods

slides.narration: In a discrete series each value occurs several times, so we multiply each value by its frequency, add the products, and divide by the total frequency. For a continuous series the class mark stands for each class. The assumed mean and step deviation methods reduce the size of the numbers, but they give exactly the same answer as the direct method.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: shoe sizes
slides.body_md: The imagined shop Step-Up Footwear sold 60 pairs in a week. Find the mean shoe size.
bullets: Step 1 — Multiply each size by its frequency: fX = 25, 60, 140, 120, 63, 30.
Step 4 — A mean size need not be a real size; here it is a figure for comparison.

visual.alt: Table of the shoe sizes 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 10 and the pairs sold 5, 10, 20, 15, 7, 3 at the imagined Step-Up Footwear, with products fX totalling 438 and 60 pairs
visual.caption: Imagined Step-Up Footwear, one week.

slides.narration: Multiply each shoe size by the number of pairs sold in that size. The products add up to 438. The total number of pairs is 60. So the mean size is 438 divided by 60, which is 7.3. Notice that no one can buy a shoe of this size, which tells us the mean is not always the best guide.

slides.heading: Quick check: mean of a discrete series
slides.body_md: Marks of pupils in a quiz are given with frequencies. Find the mean mark.
slides.narration: Multiply each mark by the number of pupils who got it. Add the products, and divide by the total number of pupils. Give the answer correct to two decimal places.

slides.heading: Continuous series: direct method
slides.body_md: Take the **class mark** of each class: m = (lower limit + upper limit) ÷ 2. Then X̄ = Σfm ÷ Σf.

visual.alt: Table of the weekly wages of 50 workers of the imagined Tarapur Cable Works in six classes with class marks 550, 650, 750, 850, 950, 1050 and fm totalling 39900
visual.caption: Imagined Tarapur Cable Works.

slides.narration: A factory called Tarapur Cable Works pays its fifty workers weekly wages that are grouped in classes of width one hundred. We take the middle of each class, the class mark, as the value of every worker in it. Multiply each class mark by its frequency and add. The total is 39900. Divide by fifty workers.

slides.heading: Assumed-mean and step-deviation methods
slides.body_md: Take **A** near the middle, find d = m − A, and for the step deviation divide by the class width: d′ = d ÷ h. X̄ = A + (Σfd′ ÷ Σf) × h.

visual.alt: Table of deviations for the Tarapur wages with an assumed mean of 850: Σfd is -2600 and, with d′ = d ÷ 100, Σfd′ is -26
visual.caption: Assumed mean 850, class width 100.

slides.narration: We take eight hundred and fifty as the assumed mean. The deviations of the class marks are small numbers, and when we divide them by the class width of one hundred they become tiny whole numbers. This makes the multiplication easy. Finally the average deviation must be multiplied back by the class width and added to the assumed mean.

slides.heading: Worked example 3: three methods, one answer
slides.body_md: Find the mean weekly wage at Tarapur Cable Works by all three methods.
bullets: Step 4 — The three results agree, which is a good check on the working.

visual.alt: Table showing that the direct, assumed-mean and step-deviation methods all give a mean weekly wage of Rs 798 for the imagined Tarapur Cable Works
visual.caption: Three methods, one answer.

slides.narration: By the direct method the mean wage is 798 rupees. By the assumed mean method we get the same figure. The step deviation method also gives 798. The three methods are only different ways of doing the same sum, so they must agree. If they do not, there is an error in the working.

slides.heading: Weighted arithmetic mean
slides.body_md: When items differ in **importance**, give each a **weight** W. Weighted mean = ΣWX ÷ ΣW.

rows: Important in proportion to its weight
Subjects with different marks, items in a household basket

visual.alt: Table comparing the simple arithmetic mean with the weighted arithmetic mean on formula, how items are treated and when each suits

slides.narration: The simple mean treats every item as equally important. Often that is not fair. A subject that carries more marks should count for more in an overall result, and a commodity that households buy more of should count for more in a price basket. We multiply each value by its weight, add, and divide by the total of the weights.

slides.heading: Worked example 4: a learner's weighted marks
slides.body_md: An imagined learner, Meera, has marks in four subjects with different weights. Find her weighted mean.
bullets: Step 4 — The simple mean is 65, lower, because her best marks carry more weight.

visual.alt: Table of the marks 80, 70, 60, 50 of the imagined learner Meera in Mathematics, Science, English and Hindi with weights 4, 3, 2, 1; ΣWX is 700 and ΣW is 10
visual.caption: Weighted mean 70 against a simple mean of 65.

slides.narration: Meera scored well in the subjects with higher weights. Her weighted total is 700 and the weights add to 10, so her weighted mean is 70. The simple mean of her four marks is only 65, because it treats every subject as equally important.

slides.heading: Quick check: weighted mean
slides.body_md: Find the weighted mean mark of another imagined learner.
slides.narration: Multiply each mark by the weight of its subject. Add the products and divide by the total of the weights. Do not divide by the number of subjects.

visual.caption: Imagined Dhunmarg rainfall: the mean is the balance point, and deviations on the two sides cancel

slides.narration: Imagine the rainfall values as equal weights on a beam. The mean is the point where the beam balances. The days below the mean have deviations that add up to minus 17, and the days above have deviations that add up to plus 17. They cancel exactly, so the sum of deviations from the mean is always zero.

slides.heading: Extreme values pull the mean
slides.body_md: The mean uses **every** value, so one very large or very small value moves it. The **median** does not move.

visual.alt: Table showing that one extreme value changes the mean but not the median: Dhunmarg rainfall mean 11 becomes 16 while the median stays 10.5; stall sales mean 50 becomes 70 while the median stays 50
visual.caption: One extreme value moves the mean, not the median.

slides.narration: When one rainy day of twenty millimetres is replaced by seventy, the mean rises from 11 to 16. The middle value does not change at all. The same happens with the sales of fruit stalls. One unusual figure pulls the mean towards it, so the mean can be a poor guide when the data have an extreme value.

slides.heading: Quick check: deviations
slides.body_md: What is the sum of the deviations of a set of values from their mean?
slides.narration: Think of the balance point. Deviations below the mean are negative and those above are positive. Decide what their total must be.

slides.heading: Merits and demerits of the mean
slides.body_md: The mean is the most widely used average, but it must be used with care.

rows: Cannot be found exactly with open-ended classes
May not be a value that occurs in the data, such as 7.3 for shoe sizes

visual.alt: Table of merits and demerits of the arithmetic mean

slides.narration: The mean is easy to understand and calculate, it uses every observation, and many further calculations are built on it. But it is affected by extreme values, it cannot be found exactly when a class is open ended, and it may not be a value that actually occurs in the data, like a mean shoe size that nobody can buy.

slides.heading: Summary of Part 1

rows: One value that represents a whole set of data
Sum of the observations over their number
Direct, assumed mean, step deviation: all give the same result
Use class marks for the values
ΣWX ÷ ΣW when items differ in importance
Deviations from the mean add to zero; extreme values pull the mean

visual.alt: Summary table of Part 1: average, mean, three methods, continuous series, weighted mean and properties of the mean

slides.narration: To recap. An average is one value that represents the whole data. The arithmetic mean is the sum divided by the number of items. For discrete series multiply by frequencies, and for continuous series use class marks. The direct, assumed mean and step deviation methods agree. A weighted mean uses weights. Deviations from the mean add to zero, and extreme values pull the mean.

slides.heading: Exam tips
bullets: Write the **formula** first, then substitute and show each step.
For a continuous series, **find the class marks** before doing anything else.
Use **assumed mean or step deviation** for large figures, and check one against the direct method.
In a weighted mean, divide by **ΣW**, not by the number of items.
Say which values are **extreme** before you trust a mean.
slides.narration: Some tips. Write the formula first, then substitute and show each step. For a continuous series, find the class marks before anything else. Use the assumed mean or step deviation method for large figures, and check against the direct method when you can. In a weighted mean divide by the total of the weights. And look for extreme values before you trust the mean.

decks.title: Measures of Central Tendency — Part 2: Median, Mode and Choosing an Average
goals: Calculate the median of individual, discrete and continuous series
Calculate the mode of individual, discrete and continuous series and locate it on a histogram
Explain why the median is a positional average and is not affected by extreme values
Choose among the mean, median and mode for a given situation

slides.heading: Median and Mode
slides.body_md: Part 2 — the **middle** value, the **commonest** value, and which average to **use**.

nodes.label: Median of individual and discrete series

visual.alt: Route map of Part 2: median of individual and discrete series, median of a continuous series, the mode, the mode on a histogram and choosing the average
visual.caption: Part 2 at a glance

slides.narration: The mean is not the only average. In this part we learn the median, which is the middle value, and the mode, which is the most common value. We calculate each for individual, discrete and continuous series, find them from graphs, and finally learn how to choose the right average for a given situation.

slides.heading: The median: the middle value
slides.body_md: The **median** is the middle value of a series arranged in order. It divides the series into **two equal parts**. For an individual series with N items it is the value of the ((N + 1) ÷ 2)th item.

visual.alt: Table of the seven arranged incomes 18, 20, 22, 24, 26, 28, 100 thousand rupees of the imagined Chandanpur hamlet; the median is the 4th item, 24
visual.caption: Seven items: the median is the 4th.

slides.narration: The median is the middle value of a series arranged in order, with half the items on each side. Here are seven incomes from an imagined hamlet, Chandanpur, arranged from lowest to highest. With seven items the middle one is the fourth, so the median income is 24 thousand rupees.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: odd and even numbers of items
slides.body_md: Find the median of the Chandanpur incomes and of the Dhunmarg rainfall.
bullets: Step 1 — Incomes: N = 7, position (7 + 1) ÷ 2 = 4th, so the median is **24**.
Step 3 — N = 10 is even, so take the average of the 5th and 6th items.

visual.alt: Table of the median of an odd and an even number of items: Chandanpur incomes have a median of 24 at the 4th place; Dhunmarg rainfall, arranged as 5, 6, 8, 9, 10, 11, 12, 14, 15, 20, has a median of 10.5
visual.caption: Odd N: one middle item. Even N: average of the two middle items.

slides.narration: Always arrange the values first. With seven incomes the median is the fourth, 24 thousand. With ten rainfall figures there is no single middle item. The fifth and sixth items are 10 and 11, so the median is their average, 10.5 millimetres. The median need not be one of the observed values.

slides.heading: Median of a discrete series
slides.body_md: Add a **cumulative frequency** column. The median is the value whose cumulative frequency first reaches ((N + 1) ÷ 2).

visual.alt: Table of shoe sizes 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 10 with pairs 5, 10, 20, 15, 7, 3 and cumulative frequencies 5, 15, 35, 50, 57, 60 for the imagined Step-Up Footwear
visual.caption: Imagined Step-Up Footwear.

slides.narration: In a discrete series the items are already grouped, so we cannot count down the list one by one. Instead we add up the frequencies as we go down the table. These are the cumulative frequencies. The median is the size whose cumulative frequency first reaches the position of the middle item.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: median shoe size
slides.body_md: Find the median size of the 60 pairs sold by the imagined Step-Up Footwear.
bullets: Step 1 — N = 60, so the median position is (60 + 1) ÷ 2 = 30.5.
Step 3 — The 30th and 31th items both fall in the group that reaches 35.

rows: First cumulative frequency of 30.5 or more is 35

visual.alt: Table of the median shoe size of the imagined Step-Up Footwear: 60 pairs, position 30.5, found at size 7
visual.caption: The 30th and 31st items both lie in the same size.

slides.narration: There are 60 pairs, so the middle lies between the 30th and 31th pairs. The cumulative frequency passes 31 at size 7, since the sizes before it add up to only 15 pairs. So both middle pairs are of size 7, and that is the median.

slides.heading: Quick check: median of a discrete series
slides.body_md: Find the median mark of the pupils in the quiz.
slides.narration: First add the frequencies to get cumulative frequencies. Then find the position of the middle items. With an even number of pupils, the median is the average of two middle marks.

slides.heading: Median of a continuous series
slides.body_md: Median = L + ((N ÷ 2 − c.f.) ÷ f) × h, where the **median class** is the first class whose cumulative frequency reaches N ÷ 2.

visual.alt: Table of the Tarapur weekly wage classes 500 to 600, 600 to 700, 700 to 800, 800 to 900, 900 to 1000, 1000 to 1100 with frequencies 4, 8, 14, 12, 8, 4 and cumulative frequencies 4, 12, 26, 38, 46, 50
visual.caption: N = 50, N ÷ 2 = 25.

slides.narration: For a continuous series we use half the total, not the position plus one over two. Here the fifty Tarapur workers give a half of twenty five. The first class whose cumulative frequency reaches twenty five is the median class. The formula then places the median inside that class, in proportion to how far we must go beyond the earlier classes.

slides.heading: Worked example 3: the median weekly wage
slides.body_md: Find the median weekly wage of the 50 workers of the imagined Tarapur Cable Works.
bullets: Step 2 — Median class: **700 to 800**, with L = 700, c.f. = 12, f = 14, h = 100.

rows: First class with cumulative frequency of 25 or more

visual.alt: Table of the median weekly wage of the imagined Tarapur Cable Works: half the workers is 25, the median class is 700 to 800, and the median is Rs 792.86
visual.caption: Median in rupees.

slides.narration: Half of the fifty workers is twenty five. The cumulative frequency before the median class is 12, so we still need 13 more workers out of the 14 in the median class. That is a fraction of the class width of 100. Adding it to the lower limit 700 gives a median wage of 792.86 rupees.

slides.heading: The median is a positional average
slides.body_md: The median depends on the **position** of the middle item, not on how large the extreme values are.

visual.alt: Table showing which of the mean, median and mode depends on what and whether each is affected by extreme values

slides.narration: The median is called a positional average because it is fixed by the position of the middle item. If the largest value becomes ten times bigger, the middle position does not change, so the median does not change. The mean depends on every value, so it moves. The mode depends only on which value is most frequent, so extreme values do not affect it either.

slides.heading: The mode: the most frequent value
slides.body_md: The **mode** is the value that occurs most often. In a discrete series it is the value with the **highest frequency**.

visual.alt: Table of shoe sizes sold in one hour at an imagined counter, 7, 8, 6, 7, 9, 7, 8, 6, 7, 10, 8, 7, counted by size; size 7 occurs 5 times and is the mode
visual.caption: Imagined Step-Up Footwear counter.

slides.narration: The mode is the value that occurs most often. At a shoe counter, the sizes sold in one hour were counted, and size 7 came up 5 times, more than any other. So the mode is 7. A shopkeeper who wants to stock the right size needs the mode, not the mean. A series may have two modes, or none.

slides.heading: Quick check: modal class
slides.body_md: Identify the modal class from a table of mango weights.
slides.narration: The modal class is the class with the highest frequency. Look down the frequency column, find the largest figure, and read off the class beside it.

slides.heading: Mode of a continuous series
slides.body_md: Mode = L + (D1 ÷ (D1 + D2)) × h, where D1 = f1 − f0 and D2 = f1 − f2 and f1 is the **modal frequency**.

visual.alt: Table of the Tarapur wage classes and frequencies 4, 8, 14, 12, 8, 4; the modal class is 700 to 800 with 14 workers, between 8 before it and 12 after it
visual.caption: The modal class has the highest frequency.

slides.narration: For a continuous series we first find the modal class, the one with the highest frequency, which here has 14 workers. Its neighbours have 8 and 12. The formula uses the differences between the modal frequency and these two neighbours. The mode is placed inside the modal class, closer to the neighbour that is larger.

notes.title: Measures of Central Tendency — Notes

sections.heading: 1. What an average is
sections.body_md:
An **average** is a single value that represents a whole set of data. In most data the values gather around a central value, which is why averages are called measures of **central tendency**. The three common averages are the arithmetic mean, the median and the mode.

Which average to use depends on the series. The mean uses every value, the median is the middle value of the arranged series, and the mode is the value that occurs most often.

key_terms.definition_md: A single value that represents a whole set of data.
The tendency of the values of a series to gather around a central value.

rows: Sum of the values over their number
Middle value of the arranged series

sections.heading: 2. Arithmetic mean: individual and discrete series
sections.body_md:
The **arithmetic mean** is the sum of all the observations divided by their number.

**Individual series, direct method:** X̄ = ΣX ÷ N. **Assumed-mean method:** X̄ = A + Σd ÷ N, with d = X − A. For the imagined Dhunmarg rainfall, ΣX = 110 and N = 10, so the mean is 11 mm; with A = 10, Σd = 10 and the mean is the same.

**Discrete series:** X̄ = ΣfX ÷ Σf. For the imagined Step-Up Footwear sales, ΣfX = 438 and Σf = 60, so the mean size is 7.3.

key_terms.definition_md: The sum of all the observations divided by their number.
A convenient value A chosen near the middle of the data, from which deviations are measured.
The difference between an observation and a chosen value, d = X − A.

sections.heading: 3. Arithmetic mean: continuous series
sections.body_md:
In a continuous series the **class mark** m = (lower limit + upper limit) ÷ 2 stands for every item of the class.

**Direct method:** X̄ = Σfm ÷ Σf. **Assumed-mean method:** X̄ = A + Σfd ÷ Σf, d = m − A. **Step-deviation method:** X̄ = A + (Σfd′ ÷ Σf) × h, d′ = (m − A) ÷ h, h the common class width.

For the imagined Tarapur Cable Works wages (50 workers) all three methods give 798 rupees: Σfm = 39900; with A = 850, Σfd = -2600; with h = 100, Σfd′ = -26.

key_terms.definition_md: The mid-point of a class, (lower limit + upper limit) ÷ 2.
A method in which deviations are divided by the common class width to make them small whole numbers.

sections.heading: 4. Weighted mean, properties, merits and demerits
sections.body_md:
The **weighted arithmetic mean** is X̄w = ΣWX ÷ ΣW, used when items differ in importance. For an imagined learner with marks 80, 70, 60, 50 and weights 4, 3, 2, 1, the weighted mean is 70 and the simple mean 65.

**Properties.** (1) The sum of the deviations from the mean is zero: for the Dhunmarg rainfall the deviations below the mean add to -17 and those above to +17. (2) The mean is affected by extreme values: replacing 20 by 70 raises the Dhunmarg mean from 11 to 16.

**Merits:** easy to understand and compute; uses every value; basis of further calculation. **Demerits:** affected by extreme values; cannot be found exactly with open-ended classes; may not be an actual value of the data.

key_terms.definition_md: A mean in which each value is multiplied by a weight showing its importance, ΣWX ÷ ΣW.
A value far larger or smaller than most of the others.

sections.heading: 5. Median
sections.body_md:
The **median** is the middle value of a series arranged in order, dividing it into two equal parts. It is a **positional average**.

**Individual series:** the value of the ((N + 1) ÷ 2)th item; for even N take the average of the two middle items (Dhunmarg rainfall, 10 days: 10.5 mm).

**Discrete series:** form cumulative frequencies and find the value in which the ((N + 1) ÷ 2)th item falls (Step-Up Footwear: size 7).

**Continuous series:** Median = L + ((N ÷ 2 − c.f.) ÷ f) × h, where L is the lower limit of the median class, c.f. the cumulative frequency before it, f its frequency and h its width. For the Tarapur wages the median is 792.86 rupees. The median can also be read from the point where the less than and more than ogives meet. It is not affected by extreme values.

key_terms.definition_md: The middle value of a series arranged in order, which divides it into two equal parts.
An average fixed by the position of an item in the arranged series rather than by all the values.
The first class whose cumulative frequency is N ÷ 2 or more.

sections.heading: 6. Mode
sections.body_md:
The **mode** is the value that occurs most frequently. In an individual or discrete series it is the value with the highest frequency (shoe size 7 at the imagined counter). A series may have more than one mode, or none.

**Continuous series:** the modal class has the highest frequency, and Mode = L + (D1 ÷ (D1 + D2)) × h, with D1 = f1 − f0, D2 = f1 − f2, f1 the modal frequency and f0, f2 the frequencies of the classes before and after it. For the Tarapur wages D1 = 6, D2 = 2 and the mode is 775 rupees.

**On a histogram:** join the top corners of the modal bar to the neighbouring corners as shown; the wage below the crossing is the mode (775).

sections.heading: 7. Choosing the average
sections.body_md:
Use the **median** when a few values are extreme, as in the imagined Chandanpur hamlet where one family's income pulls the mean to 34 thousand while the median is 24 thousand. Use the **mode** for the most popular item, such as the shoe size to stock. Use the **arithmetic mean** when every value should count, as for the marks of a class, and a **weighted mean** when items differ in importance.

When the mean, median and mode are far apart, the data have an extreme value or are lopsided, and the choice must be explained.

notes.exam_tips_md:
- Write the **formula** first, then substitute; show every step.
- For a continuous series find **class marks** (mean) or the **median class / modal class** first.
- Check the assumed-mean or step-deviation answer against the direct method.
- In a weighted mean divide by **ΣW**.
- Arrange data in order before finding a median; for even N average the two middle items.
- Give a **reason** whenever you choose an average.

cards.back_md: A single value that represents a whole set of data.
The tendency of the values of a series to gather around a central value.
The sum of all the observations divided by their number.

cards.front_md: Mean of an individual series, **direct method**
cards.back_md: X̄ = ΣX ÷ N.

cards.front_md: Mean of an individual series, **assumed-mean method**
cards.back_md: X̄ = A + Σd ÷ N, where d = X − A.
X̄ = ΣfX ÷ Σf.
The mid-point of a class: (lower limit + upper limit) ÷ 2.

cards.front_md: Mean of a continuous series, **direct method**
cards.back_md: X̄ = Σfm ÷ Σf, with m the class mark.

cards.front_md: Mean of a continuous series, **assumed-mean method**
cards.back_md: X̄ = A + Σfd ÷ Σf, with d = m − A.

cards.front_md: Mean of a continuous series, **step-deviation method**
cards.back_md: X̄ = A + (Σfd′ ÷ Σf) × h, with d′ = (m − A) ÷ h.

cards.front_md: Do the **three methods** of finding the mean agree?
cards.back_md: Yes. They are different ways of doing the same sum and must give the same mean.
To work with smaller numbers; the answer does not change.
ΣWX ÷ ΣW: each value is multiplied by a weight showing its importance.
When the items differ in importance, as subjects carrying different marks.

cards.front_md: Sum of the **deviations** from the mean
cards.back_md: Always zero.
The mean is affected by extreme values, because it uses every observation.
Easy to understand and calculate; uses every observation.
Affected by extreme values; cannot be found exactly with open-ended classes.
The middle value of a series arranged in order, dividing it into two equal parts.
The value of the ((N + 1) ÷ 2)th item; for even N the average of the two middle items.
Use cumulative frequencies to find the value in which the ((N + 1) ÷ 2)th item falls.
The first class whose cumulative frequency is N ÷ 2 or more.

cards.front_md: Why is the median a **positional average**?
cards.back_md: It is fixed by the position of the middle item, so extreme values do not affect it.

cards.front_md: Where do the **ogives** show the median?
cards.back_md: At the point where the less than and more than ogives cross.
The value that occurs most frequently in a series.
The class with the highest frequency in a continuous series.
L + (D1 ÷ (D1 + D2)) × h, with D1 = f1 − f0 and D2 = f1 − f2.
Join the top corners of the modal bar to the neighbouring bars across; read the value below the crossing.

cards.front_md: Which average for a **typical income** with an extreme value?
cards.back_md: The median.

cards.front_md: Which average for the **most popular size**?
cards.back_md: The mode.

cards.front_md: Which average when **every value should count**?
cards.back_md: The arithmetic mean, or a weighted mean when items differ in importance.

questions.stem_md: A statistician says that the average weekly wage of the workers of the imagined Tarapur Cable Works is Rs 798. In statistics an average is

options.text_md: the largest value in the data
a single value that represents the whole set of data
the difference between the largest and the smallest value
the number of observations in the data

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** a single value that represents the whole set of data. An average sums up a whole distribution in one representative value that lies near its centre. The largest value, the range and the count of observations do not represent the group as a whole.

questions.stem_md: The imagined Kaladhar hill station recorded rainfall of 6, 9, 12, 4, 15, 8, 10, 12 millimetres over 8 days. The arithmetic mean of these observations is obtained by

options.text_md: dividing the largest observation by the number of observations
taking the value in the middle after arranging them in order
taking the value that occurs most often
dividing the sum of the observations by their number

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** dividing the sum of the observations by their number. The arithmetic mean is the sum of all observations divided by how many there are. Taking the middle value gives the median, and the most frequent value is the mode.

questions.stem_md: For an individual series with an assumed mean A, deviations d = X − A and N observations, the arithmetic mean by the assumed-mean method is

options.text_md: A + Σd / N
A − Σd / N
A × Σd / N
Σd / (A × N)

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** A + Σd / N. Each X is A + d, so the sum of X is N times A plus Σd, and dividing by N gives A + Σd / N. The other expressions do not reduce to ΣX / N.

questions.stem_md: In the step-deviation method for a continuous series with assumed mean A, class width h and d′ = (m − A) / h, the mean is

options.text_md: A + Σfd′ / Σf
A + (Σfd′ × h) / A
A + (Σfd′ / Σf) × h
h + (Σfd′ / Σf) × A

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** A + (Σfd′ / Σf) × h. Because d′ was divided by h, the average of d′ must be multiplied back by h before it is added to A. Leaving out h, or swapping the roles of h and A, gives a wrong mean.

questions.stem_md: The mean of the five weekly sales 12, 15, 9, 18, 6 (in crates) of an imagined fruit stall is 12. The sum of the deviations of these five values from their mean is

options.text_md: zero
negative

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** zero. The deviations are 0, 3, -3, 6, -6; the positive and negative ones cancel and add to 0, which is true of every series. 12 is the mean itself and 60 is the sum of the observations, not of the deviations.

questions.stem_md: The monthly incomes of seven families of the imagined Chandanpur hamlet are 18, 20, 22, 24, 26, 28, 100 thousand rupees. Which statement about the arithmetic mean is correct?

options.text_md: It is 34 thousand, pulled up by the one very high income
It is 24 thousand, the middle income
It is 23 thousand, the same as without the highest income
It cannot be calculated for such unequal incomes

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** It is 34 thousand, pulled up by the one very high income. The mean uses every value: 238 ÷ 7 = 34. The 24 thousand figure is the median, 23 would be the mean only if the highest income were dropped, and a mean can be found for any numerical data.

questions.stem_md: To find the mean of a continuous series by the direct method for the imagined Vidyamandir Evening School, the value taken to represent the class 40 to 50 is

options.text_md: 40, the lower limit
50, the upper limit
10, the class width
45, the class mark

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** 45, the class mark. Every item of a class is taken to be at its mid-point, the class mark, which is (lower limit + upper limit) ÷ 2. Using a limit or the width would shift the mean wrongly.

questions.stem_md: A weighted arithmetic mean is preferred to the simple mean when

options.text_md: the data have an even number of items
the items in the data differ in importance
the data contain a repeated value
the data are written in class intervals

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** the items in the data differ in importance. Weights express the relative importance of the items, as when a subject carries more marks or a price matters more in a household basket. Even counts, repeated values and class intervals do not call for weights.

questions.stem_md: The wages of workers of an imagined firm are grouped in classes that end with an open class, Rs 1,000 and above. The arithmetic mean cannot be found exactly because

options.text_md: the class mark of the open class cannot be calculated without assuming a limit
the mean can be found only when every class has a frequency of at least ten
open classes always have zero frequency
the mean needs the items to be in ascending order

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** the class mark of the open class cannot be calculated without assuming a limit. The mean needs a class mark for every class, and an open class has no upper limit, so one would have to be assumed. Frequencies and ordering are not the difficulty here.

questions.stem_md: The daily sales of an imagined tea stall on five days are 8, 10, 12, 14, 16 cups, with a mean of 12. If each day's sale were 5 cups more, the new mean would be
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** 17. Adding a constant to every observation adds the same constant to the mean: 12 + 5 = 17. The mean does not stay the same, is not multiplied by 5, and 65 confuses the sum with the mean.

questions.stem_md: The assumed-mean method is preferred to the direct method for a series with large values mainly because

options.text_md: it gives a more accurate mean than the direct method
it avoids the use of frequencies
it reduces the size of the numbers to be multiplied and added
it can be used only for large data

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** it reduces the size of the numbers to be multiplied and added. Deviations from a convenient A are small, so the arithmetic is lighter, but the result is exactly the same as by the direct method. It does not give a different or more accurate mean, and frequencies are still used.

questions.stem_md: The median of the monthly marks of the learners of an imagined class, after the marks are arranged in order, is

options.text_md: the sum of the marks divided by the number of learners
the mark obtained by the largest number of learners
the difference between the highest and the lowest marks
the middle value, which divides the series into two equal parts

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** the middle value, which divides the series into two equal parts. The median is the middle item of an arranged series, with half the items on either side. The other three descriptions are the mean, the mode and the range.

questions.stem_md: The weekly wages of 31 workers of an imagined mill are arranged in ascending order. The median is the value of the

options.text_md: 15.5th item
31st item
8th item
16th item

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** 16th item. For an odd number of items the median is the ((N + 1) ÷ 2)th item, that is (31 + 1) ÷ 2 = 16. Half of 31 is not a whole item number, 31st is the largest item, and a quarter point is not the median.

questions.stem_md: The ages (years) of eight members of the imagined Green Park Cycling Club, arranged in order, are 11, 15, 18, 22, 26, 30, 34, 45. The median age is

options.text_md: 22 years
26 years
24 years
25.13 years

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** 24 years. With eight items the median is the average of the 4th and 5th items: (22 + 26) ÷ 2 = 24. Taking only the 4th or only the 5th item is incomplete, and 25.13 is the mean.

questions.stem_md: To find the median size from a discrete series of shoe sizes and the number of pairs sold in the imagined Rapid Footwear Mart, the most helpful column to add is the

options.text_md: product of size and frequency
cumulative frequency
class mark
difference of successive frequencies

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** cumulative frequency. The cumulative frequency tells which size contains the middle item. The product of size and frequency is used for the mean, a class mark belongs to continuous series, and differences of frequencies help in locating the mode of classes.

questions.stem_md: In the formula Median = L + ((N / 2 − c.f.) / f) × h for a continuous series, c.f. stands for

options.text_md: the cumulative frequency of the class before the median class
the cumulative frequency of the median class itself
the frequency of the median class
the class factor, the same as the class width

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** the cumulative frequency of the class before the median class. The median class is found where the cumulative frequency first reaches N / 2, and c.f. is the total of the frequencies of all classes before it. The frequency of the median class is f, and h is the class width.

questions.stem_md: The weekly sales (crates) of five imagined stalls are 40, 45, 50, 55, 60. If the last stall's sale is recorded wrongly as 160, which measure stays at 50?

options.text_md: the arithmetic mean
the median
the sum of the sales
the average of the smallest and the largest sale

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** the median. The median depends on the position of the middle item, which is the third, and the extreme value does not change its position, so it stays 50. The mean moves from 50 to 70, and the sum and the average of the extremes also change.

questions.stem_md: In a record of the shoe sizes bought from the imagined Step-Up Footwear in one day, the mode is the

options.text_md: average of all the sizes
middle size after arranging in order
difference between the largest and the smallest size
size that occurs most frequently

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** size that occurs most frequently. The mode is the most frequently occurring value. The average is the mean, the middle value is the median, and the difference of extremes is the range.

questions.stem_md: The imagined Step-Up Footwear owner wants to order most pairs in the size that sells best. The sizes sold in one hour are 7, 8, 6, 7, 9, 7, 8, 6, 7, 10, 8, 7. She should order for the size

options.text_md: 7, the mode
7.5, the mean
7, the median
10, the largest

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** 7, the mode. The size sold most often, 7, is the mode, and it is the right guide for stocking. A mean of 7.5 is not even a size that exists, and the largest size is the least useful guide.

questions.stem_md: The mango weights (grams) of the imagined Maple Orchard are grouped as 200 to 250: 3; 250 to 300: 8; 300 to 350: 14; 350 to 400: 12; 400 to 450: 3. The modal class is
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** 300 to 350. The modal class is the class with the highest frequency, 14 here, which is 300 to 350. The 350 to 400 class has 12 mangoes and the others have fewer.

questions.stem_md: In the formula Mode = L + (D1 / (D1 + D2)) × h for a continuous series with equal classes, D1 is

options.text_md: the frequency of the modal class minus the frequency of the class after it
the frequency of the modal class itself
the frequency of the modal class minus the frequency of the class before it
the width of the modal class

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** the frequency of the modal class minus the frequency of the class before it. D1 = f1 − f0, taking the modal class frequency less that of the preceding class. D2 is the same with the following class, and h is the class width.

questions.stem_md: A report on the incomes of seven families of the imagined Chandanpur hamlet, 18, 20, 22, 24, 26, 28, 100 thousand rupees, has to state a typical income. The best choice is

options.text_md: the median, 24 thousand, because one very high income distorts the mean
the mean, 34 thousand, because it uses every value
the mode, because every income occurs only once
the largest income, since it shows the maximum earnings

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** the median, 24 thousand, because one very high income distorts the mean. With one extreme income, the median 24 stays near what most families earn while the mean 34 is dragged upward. The mode does not exist, and the largest income is not typical.

questions.stem_md: The less than and more than ogives of the weekly wages of the 50 workers of the imagined Tarapur Cable Works are drawn on one graph. At the point where they cross, the cumulative frequency is

options.text_md: 50, which is N
51, which is N + 1
zero
25, which is N / 2

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** 25, which is N / 2. At the median, half the items lie below and half above, so each ogive reads N / 2 = 25. A reading of 50 is the top of the less than curve, and the curves never read 51 or zero at their crossing.

questions.stem_md: To locate the mode of a continuous series from its histogram, the two lines drawn from the modal bar meet. The mode is read

options.text_md: on the vertical axis across from their meeting point
on the horizontal axis directly below their meeting point
at the top of the tallest bar
at the midpoint of the base of the modal bar

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** on the horizontal axis directly below their meeting point. The vertical line from the meeting point of the two joining lines cuts the horizontal axis at the mode. The vertical axis shows frequency, the top of the bar shows only the modal frequency, and the midpoint of the base would ignore the neighbouring bars.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** The median of a series is not changed when its largest value is replaced by a much larger one.

**Reason (R):** The median is a positional average, determined by the middle item of the arranged series and not by the size of the extreme values.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Both are true and R explains A. The middle position is the same after the largest value grows, so the median is untouched.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** The arithmetic mean is affected by extreme values.

**Reason (R):** The algebraic sum of the deviations of the observations from their mean is zero.

Choose the correct option.
